questions.q: What does Nmap's default TCP SYN scan (-sS) actually do when it finds an open port?
options: It opens a raw socket and leaves it connected for the rest of the scan
It sends a SYN, receives a SYN/ACK, and sends a RST instead of completing the handshake
It downloads the service banner before reporting the port as open
It completes a full TCP three-way handshake and keeps the connection open
questions.explain: A SYN scan is 'half-open': Nmap sends a SYN, reads the SYN/ACK as confirmation the port is open, then sends a RST instead of finishing the handshake, so a full connection is never established.

questions.q: A scanned port returns no response at all, and no ICMP error either. How does Nmap report its state?
options: closed
open
filtered
Nmap refuses to report anything and skips the port
questions.explain: No response (or an ICMP unreachable) means Nmap can't confirm the port's real state — it reports 'filtered,' which usually means a firewall is dropping the probe, not that the port is confirmed closed.

questions.q: Why would a pentester use -sT (TCP connect scan) instead of the default -sS?
options: -sT is always faster than -sS on every network
-sT is required for scanning UDP ports
-sT doesn't need raw-socket privileges, which -sS requires
-sT automatically evades every firewall that -sS cannot
questions.explain: -sT completes the full handshake through the OS socket API, so it works without root/Administrator privileges — the tradeoff is that it's logged more visibly on the target side than a half-open SYN scan.

questions.q: A SYN scan reports 93% confidence for a specific OS guess. What's the correct way to treat that number?
options: As a statistical fingerprint match that should be verified, not cited as a confirmed fact
As definitive proof of the exact OS build running on the host
As irrelevant, since OS fingerprinting is never useful during a pentest
As a guarantee that the host has no further patches applied
questions.explain: -O compares TCP/IP stack quirks against a fingerprint database and returns a statistical match with a confidence score. Hardened or load-balanced hosts can return low-confidence or outright wrong guesses, so it informs assumptions rather than confirming them.

questions.q: What is the real tradeoff being made when choosing a slower Nmap timing template like -T1 over -T4?
options: Slower timing scans more ports per probe, giving more complete results
Slower timing guarantees the scan will find vulnerabilities that faster scans miss
Slower timing uses less bandwidth but always produces identical port results to -T4
Slower timing reduces the chance of tripping IDS alerting thresholds, at the cost of a scan that takes far longer to finish
questions.explain: Timing templates pace probes to balance speed against detectability. A paranoid setting like -T0/-T1 can take hours but is far less likely to trigger IDS alerting or stress a fragile host; -T4/-T5 finish fast but generate an easily detected burst of traffic.
